mcqs.question: A process divides by zero and the CPU immediately hands control to the kernel. What category of event is this?
options: An exception, since it's synchronous and caused by the instruction currently executing
An interrupt, since it stops normal execution
A trap, since the program indirectly asked for it
None of these — divide-by-zero is handled entirely in user mode
mcqs.explanation: Divide-by-zero is a textbook exception: it's synchronous and caused directly by the instruction the CPU was executing, not by an external device (interrupt) or a deliberate request (trap). It can't be handled purely in user mode since the CPU can't safely continue.

mcqs.question: How does the CPU find the correct handler when an interrupt fires?
options: It asks the currently running process which handler to use
It looks up the interrupt number as an index into the interrupt vector table (IDT on x86)
It scans all loaded drivers sequentially until one claims the interrupt
The handler address is hard-coded into every device's firmware
mcqs.explanation: The interrupt vector table is indexed directly by interrupt number, giving O(1) dispatch to the right ISR — no scanning, no asking the running process (which has no say), and no per-device hard-coded address in firmware.

mcqs.question: Why do non-maskable interrupts (NMIs) exist separately from ordinary maskable interrupts?
options: NMIs are simply a faster variant of maskable interrupts with no other difference
NMIs are used exclusively for keyboard and mouse input
Maskable interrupts are deprecated and NMIs are meant to replace them entirely
So genuinely catastrophic conditions (hardware failure, watchdog timeout) can't be suppressed even by a kernel that has disabled ordinary interrupts
mcqs.explanation: NMIs exist precisely so severe hardware conditions get handled no matter what — even during a critical section where the kernel has masked ordinary interrupts. They aren't just "faster," aren't reserved for input devices, and haven't replaced maskable interrupts, which remain the vast majority of interrupt traffic.

mcqs.question: Linux's NAPI framework switches a network driver from interrupts to polling under heavy packet load. Why?
options: At very high event rates, per-event interrupt overhead itself becomes the bottleneck, so polling in a tight loop is actually cheaper
Polling is always faster than interrupts regardless of event frequency
Interrupts stop working correctly above a certain hardware clock speed
It's a legacy workaround with no real performance benefit today
mcqs.explanation: When packets arrive extremely fast, the fixed per-interrupt overhead (handler dispatch, context save/restore) repeated for every single packet outweighs the cost of just polling in a loop — this is a genuine, still-relevant performance trade-off, not a hardware limitation or legacy leftover, and it doesn't mean polling always wins.

mcqs.question: Why does Linux split interrupt handling into a "top half" and a "bottom half" instead of doing everything in the ISR?
options: Because ISRs are not allowed to access hardware registers at all
Because a long-running ISR delays other interrupts and blocks the scheduler, so heavy work is deferred to a context where interrupts are re-enabled
Because the kernel randomly assigns work between the two halves for load balancing
Because bottom halves run on a separate physical CPU reserved for that purpose
mcqs.explanation: Keeping the ISR (top half) minimal avoids delaying other interrupts and scheduler activity; the bottom half handles the bulk of the work later with interrupts enabled again. ISRs can access hardware registers, the split isn't random load balancing, and it doesn't require a dedicated separate CPU.

mcqs.question: A page fault occurs when a process accesses an unmapped virtual address. Why is this exception usually recoverable, unlike a divide-by-zero?
options: Page faults are not actually exceptions, they're a special type of interrupt
The kernel always kills the process on any page fault, so recoverability doesn't apply
Divide-by-zero and page faults are handled by identical code paths
The kernel can map in the needed page and re-execute the exact same instruction, which then succeeds
mcqs.explanation: A page fault handler can fix the underlying condition (bring in the missing page) and safely retry the instruction, because the instruction itself was never invalid — only its data was momentarily unavailable. Divide-by-zero has no such fix, since the instruction itself can't succeed. Page faults are exceptions, not interrupts, and the two aren't handled by the same code path.
